cards.explanation: The answer is Paul's teaching and the way he lives. Timothy got the front-row seat, friends. Paul says Timothy has observed his teaching and his conduct, and then the list keeps going: purpose, faith, patience, love, perseverance (2 Timothy 3:10). Timothy didn't just hear Paul talk, he watched Paul do it. Anybody can sound good on a Sunday, but it's the Tuesday stuff that shows you.

The answer is that the Lord rescued him from all of them. Paul says, "Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them." (2 Timothy 3:11) Notice who gets the credit, friends. Paul doesn't say he was tough or clever, he says the Lord rescued him. I think that's a good thing for Timothy to hear before Paul says more about hard times.

The answer is persecuted. Paul says it straight: "Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted…" (2 Timothy 3:12). He just walked through his own stories, so he isn't guessing. It's not exactly a recruiting slogan, is it, friends? But Paul tells Timothy the truth, and the verse right before it says the Lord rescued Paul from all of it (2 Timothy 3:11).

The answer is that they go from bad to worse. Paul says, "…evil men and imposters go from bad to worse…" (2 Timothy 3:13). An imposter doesn't get better by pretending longer, friends. The direction Paul describes is downhill. It's like a cookie batch that gets a little more burnt every time it goes back in the oven.

The answer is False. Paul says it goes both ways. Evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, "…deceiving and being deceived." (2 Timothy 3:13) They're fooling others while getting fooled themselves, friends. That's one tangled mess, and Paul says it plainly.

The answer is to continue in what he has learned. Paul says, "But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed…" (2 Timothy 3:14). Imposters are going from bad to worse, and Paul's answer isn't to chase something new, friends. It's to keep going in what Timothy already learned and firmly believed. Steady wins here.

The answer is that he knows who he learned them from. Paul gives the reason right in the verse: "…since you know from whom you have learned them." (2 Timothy 3:14) Timothy knows the source of what he learned, friends. That's the reason Paul gives. Timothy can trust it because he knows who taught him.

The answer is False. Paul says, "From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures…" (2 Timothy 3:15). So Timothy's time with the Scriptures started in infancy, friends, not after he met Paul. That's what makes the statement False.

The answer is faith. Paul says the Holy Scriptures "…are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." (2 Timothy 3:15) The Scriptures make Timothy wise for salvation, friends, and that comes through faith in Christ Jesus. It's a short word carrying a big load.

The answer is that God breathed it out. That's what "God-breathed" means: "All Scripture is God-breathed…" (2 Timothy 3:16). The source is God Himself, friends. It's not a collection of good ideas somebody had. Paul puts the word ALL in front of Scripture, too.

The answer is True. Correction is on Paul's list, friends. Scripture "…is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness…" (2 Timothy 3:16). It's one of four uses. Correction isn't fun in the moment, but Paul says it's useful, and I'm not going to argue with him.

The answer is equipping the man of God for every good work. That's the goal: "…so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work." (2 Timothy 3:17) All four uses lead there, friends. Complete, fully equipped, and ready for every good work. Nothing missing from the toolbox.
